item.title: Workshop: Revisiting Surveys
item.description: This resource contains the complete material from the workshop “Revisiting Surveys”, designed to shift the analytical paradigm from the independence of observations toward structural interdependence. Content Summary The course covers 5 main modules, available on the project website: The Survey as a Complex System: Critique of the atomistic view and foundations of latent social structure (McPherson, Smith-Lovin). The Homophilic Force: Empirical estimation of demographic “weights” on the probability of social contact using personal network data (GSS 2004) and Conditional Logit models.

item.title: Deputies Dataset 2002-2026
item.description: This dataset provides ideological position estimates for members of the Chilean Chamber of Deputies across six consecutive legislative periods, spanning from 2002 to 2026 in four-year intervals. The estimates are based exclusively on roll-call votes related to bill proposals debated and voted on in the plenary sessions. It excludes other types of votes, such as those on non-binding agreements or investigative commissions, which do not directly contribute to lawmaking. item.title: Same score, different network
item.description: Composite risk instruments summarize many indicators in a single severity score. This is efficient for case management, but it hides how risk factors are organized and the fact that the same total score can be reached through different paths. This article proposes a network-based framework to study that heterogeneity among cases with equivalent scores. Data The study uses 17,272 administrative assessments from the first module of the Intervention Management Instrument (IGI, Instrumento de Gestión de Intervención), administered by Chile’s prison service (Gendarmería de Chile) between 2015 and 2022 as part of in-prison case management.

item.title: Denise Laroze
item.description: Denise Laroze is an Associate Professor at the Research Center for Social Complexity (CICS) of the School of Government at Universidad del Desarrollo. She holds a Ph.D. in Government (Political Science) from the University of Essex and an M.Sc. in Political Science and Political Economy from the London School of Economics, United Kingdom. She currently leads the Mobile Experimental Laboratory within the PoliCICS group. Her academic research specializes in behavioral science and decision-making.

item.title: LEM
item.description: About LEM The Mobile Experimental Laboratory (LEM) is a collaborative space belonging to the Research Center in Social Complexity (CICS) at Universidad del Desarrollo, in Chile. Its mission is to provide a dynamic and flexible environment for conducting innovative research addressing complex social challenges. In this laboratory, students, postdocs, academics, and national and international collaborators linked to CICS gather to work on interdisciplinary projects, all with a common focus: the use of experimental methods in social sciences.

item.title: Aníbal Olivera
item.description: Aníbal Olivera is a Ph.D. student in Social Complexity Sciences, funded by an ANID National Doctoral Scholarship. He previously trained in Physics at the Universidad de Concepción, where he earned a B.Sc. in Physics and an M.Sc. in Physics. His research studies how the structure of social networks shapes the diffusion and abandonment of behaviors. In Networks Decide for Us he imputes homophilous networks onto representative surveys to measure how much of diffusion is due to topology; in Network Disadoption he proposes a measure of exposure to neighbors who abandon a behavior; and in Political Networks he analyzes collaboration among members of Chile’s 2021-2022 Constitutional Convention.

item.title: Network Disadoption: exposure to disadoption as an indicator of social contagion
item.description: Research on the diffusion of innovations has focused on adoption: moving from not using to using a practice. Its natural counterpart, disadoption (stopping its use), has received far less attention, even though it is a substantively different process. This project asks whether abandoning a behavior also spreads through the network, and how to measure that influence. The work is carried out by Aníbal Olivera in collaboration with Thomas W. Valente and the team at the Center for Applied Network Analysis (USC).

item.title: Networks Decide for Us: network structure as a causal force in diffusion
item.description: The diffusion of collective behaviors is usually modeled as the outcome of individual decisions or as a contagion process. This project starts from a different question: if we hold each person’s propensities fixed, does diffusion change just because the shape of the network changes? The argument is that networks “decide for us”: relational structure, shaped by homophily, enables or constrains social change beyond the sum of individual preferences. The project is carried out by Aníbal Olivera and Jorge Fábrega (CICS, UDD) together with Thomas W.

item.title: Political Networks: collaboration in the Constitutional Convention (2021–2022)
item.description: Chile’s Constitutional Convention (2021–2022) is a rare natural experiment for studying how political collaboration organizes from scratch: a majority of delegates with no prior political experience, a body that dissolved upon delivering its draft, and procedural rules written by its own members. Two of those rules structure the study. Each constitutional initiative required between 8 and 16 signatures, so signing amounted to forming a visible, dated coalition. In addition, each provision needed two thirds of the plenary (103 of 154 votes) to pass.

item.title: New publication in Applied Network Science: Same score, different network
item.description: PoliCICS researchers Jorge Fábrega and Aníbal Olivera published the article “Same score, different network: configuration-level heterogeneity in composite risk measures” in Applied Network Science. The work proposes a network-based framework for examining cases that share the same risk score but may differ in how their factors are organized. Using 17,272 administrative assessments from a criminological instrument applied by Chile’s prison service (Gendarmería de Chile), the authors show that identical scores can correspond to distinct, recurrent network architectures, and that some patterns of item co-presence are associated with recidivism.

item.title: Workshop 'Revisiting Surveys' at Summer School 2026
item.description: As part of the 3rd Summer School in Social Complexity Sciences (2026), CICS researchers Jorge Fábrega and Aníbal Olivera successfully taught the workshop “Revisiting Surveys: A Social Complexity Perspective”. The course provided students and professionals with tools to analyze traditional survey data through the lens of structural interdependence, using latent network imputation models and network psychometrics. All course materials, including the website with tutorials, R code, and datasets, have been released as an open resource for the community.

Launch of Deputies Dataset 2002-2026
item.description: The PoliCICS laboratory is pleased to announce the launch of the Deputies Dataset 2002-2026, a new public resource developed by researcher Jorge Fábrega. This dataset provides systematic estimates of the ideological positions of all members of the Chilean Chamber of Deputies across six consecutive legislative periods. The estimates are based exclusively on roll-call votes related to bill proposals debated and voted on in plenary sessions, offering a robust tool for legislative analysis.

About PoliCICS
item.description: Bridging the Gap Between Sciences The traditional notion of incompatibility between social and natural sciences has historically hindered a deep understanding of social interaction. Contrary to this tradition, contemporary science has accumulated compelling evidence that social interaction is conditioned by biological, psychological, economic, and evolutionary factors. An adequate understanding of the complexity of social systems requires a multidisciplinary approach that integrates insights from distinct theoretical and methodological frameworks. Computational Social Science At PoliCICS, we model social phenomena using a diverse array of advanced techniques, making extensive use of the digital footprint left by human interactions.
